concept.name: Spring
concept.definition: The Wyckoff event in which price briefly breaks below the support of an accumulation trading range, then quickly reverses back into the range, trapping late sellers while large interests acquire remaining shares at bargain prices. It is a hypothesized bear-trap event whose bullish interpretation must be confirmed by subsequent strength; it is not a reliable standalone buy signal.
concept.intuition: A fake breakdown: price dips under support just far enough to scare out weak hands and trigger stops, then snaps right back.
concept.mechanics: Late in an accumulation range (Phase C), price pushes below the range low; the analyst watches volume and the speed of recovery. A low-volume spring that reverses and closes back inside the range indicates exhausted supply and is treated as a high-probability long entry, ideally validated by a following test and a sign of strength.
concept.failure_modes: Not every dip below range support is a spring; if heavy selling continues after the break, the 'spring' was a genuine breakdown and the range interpretation fails. Springs do not occur in every accumulation structure.
concept.misconceptions: A spring is not confirmed at the moment of the low; Wyckoff treats the low-volume recovery and subsequent test or SOS as the confirmation, and springs are optional, not required, elements of accumulation.
concept.example: A stock ranges between 90 and 102 for months, then spikes to 87 on light volume and closes at 91 the same day; the next week it rallies on widening spread, validating the spring.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
